#### How — stack and heap at every step

**What is being answered.** Why accumulation mode is a correctness setting — as three pane streams and two sinks, all five pairings computed.

`panesFor(mode)` is the pipeline: it decides what gets published for the window's two firings. `sinkSum` and `sinkReplace` are the two things a consumer can do with a pane. Neither sink can see which mode produced its input.

That is the whole lesson. Three pairings reach 19; `badSum` reaches **34** and `badRepl` reaches **4**. Every function in the listing is correct in all five cases, and the only thing that varied was an agreement nobody wrote down.

The animation steps through the code, holding each line long enough to read the STACK (call frames and their locals) and the HEAP (allocated arrays and objects) as they are AT THAT MOMENT. Expand any step to study it on its own.

The second pane is DELTA = 4, which is id 7's own `v` — not the window's 19. Cheapest to transmit, and it only means anything to a sink that adds. Read that pane in isolation and it looks like a window containing 4.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 2 of 4</b> — a summing sink reaches the right answer from those panes</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch02-how-memory/frames/step-02.svg" alt="Step 2: a summing sink reaches the right answer from those panes" width="980">

`acc` goes 0 → 15 → 19. Correct — because the sink's behaviour matches the mode. Nothing in `sinkSum` knows which mode produced its input, which is precisely why the agreement has to be made outside the code.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 3 of 4</b> — the SAME sink, given accumulating panes, double counts</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch02-how-memory/frames/step-03.svg" alt="Step 3: the SAME sink, given accumulating panes, double counts" width="980">

15 + 19 = **34** — 79% high, because pane 2 already contained pane 1. The pipeline was right, the sink was right, and the result is wrong by 15. No error is raised anywhere.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 4 of 4</b> — which is why retraction exists: an undo makes adding safe</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch02-how-memory/frames/step-04.svg" alt="Step 4: which is why retraction exists: an undo makes adding safe" width="980">

Retracting emits 15, -15, 19 — the undo `0 - ONTIME` = -15 cancels what the sink already stored, then 19 replaces it. `sinkSum` reaches 19 without being changed. Compare `badRepl` = 4: a replacing sink fed discarding panes keeps only 4, losing 15.

</details>
